content: The data regarding the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) were not considered indirect, and thus the quality of evidence was not downgraded. However, the sensitivity and specificity estimates for HPV testing and VIA showed variability despite similar cut-off values. This inconsistency could not be attributed to the quality of the studies and was therefore downgraded. This judgment was made in the context of other factors, particularly imprecision. The colposcopy data were contributed by a limited number of participants, resulting in wide confidence intervals for colposcopy specificity. This variability in confidence intervals could lead to different clinical decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. GRADE evidence for patient-important outcomes following different screen-and-treat strategies, such as HPV testing alone versus HPV testing followed by colposcopy, was evaluated. The outcomes included mortality from cervical cancer, cervical cancer incidence, recurrence of CIN 2+, undetected CIN 2+ (false negatives), major bleeding, premature delivery, infertility, major infections, minor infections, unnecessary treatment (false positives), and cancers detected at first-time screening. The data were presented per 1,000,000 patients. For example, mortality from cervical cancer was highest in the no screen group (4,350 deaths per 1,000,000) and lowest in the HPV testing followed by colposcopy group (402 deaths per 1,000,000). Similarly, cervical cancer incidence was highest in the no screen group (6,075 cases per 1,000,000) and lowest in the HPV testing followed by colposcopy group (563 cases per 1,000,000). Recurrence of CIN 2+ was consistent across most strategies, while undetected CIN 2+ (false negatives) was significant in some groups. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of HPV testing were 93% (95% CI: 87–96) and 88% (95% CI: 82–91), respectively. For colposcopic impression, the pooled sensitivity was 95% (95% CI: 82–98), but the specificity was much lower at 42% (95% CI: 26–61). The overall quality of evidence (QoE) for these outcomes was rated as very low due to the low quality of evidence for treatment effects and natural progression data. Assumptions were made for certain outcomes. For instance, no mortality from cervical cancer was assumed in true negatives (TN) and false positives (FP). Mortality in women with HIV-positive status was assumed to be the same as in women with unknown HIV status, with 250 deaths per 350 women with cervical cancer. Similarly, no cervical cancer was assumed in TN or FP cases. The incidence of cervical cancer was based on age-standardized rates from Eastern Africa, with 350 cases per 1,000,000 women, of whom 2% had CIN 2+. Major bleeding was assumed to be zero in TN and false negatives (FN) as they were not treated. However, 0.001705 of the population treated with cold knife conization (CKC) was estimated to experience major bleeding. Premature delivery was assumed to occur in 5% of the population, with 0.001705 of those treated with CKC experiencing this outcome. No data were identified regarding the risk of infertility after treatment for CIN 2+. Major infections were assumed to be zero in TN and FN cases, but 0.000888 of those treated with CKC were estimated to experience major infections. Similarly, minor infections were assumed to be zero in TN and FN cases, but 0.009368 of those treated with CKC were estimated to experience minor infections. Cancers detected at first-time screening were calculated based on data from Sankaranarayanan et al. (2005). Numbers for single screening tests were calculated as screen-detected cancers in women who participated in the screening program, while numbers for tests with colposcopy were calculated as screen-detected plus clinically detected cancers. No cancers were assumed to be found in the no screen group. The diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) evidence profile compared HPV testing alone to HPV testing followed by colposcopy with biopsy when indicated. The outcomes included true positives (patients with CIN 2+), true negatives (patients without CIN 2+), false positives (patients incorrectly classified as having CIN 2+), and false negatives (patients incorrectly classified as not having CIN 2+). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as low due to serious limitations, inconsistency, and imprecision. For true positives, the pooled sensitivity of HPV testing was 93% (95% CI: 87–96), with no absolute difference compared to HPV testing followed by colposcopy. For true negatives, the pooled specificity of HPV testing was 79.2% (95% CI: 73.8–81.9), with 108 fewer false positives compared to HPV testing followed by colposcopy. For false negatives, the pooled rate was 7% (95% CI: 4–13), with no absolute difference between the two strategies. The evidence was assessed using the QUADAS tool to evaluate the risk of bias. Many studies only performed one biopsy of an abnormal lesion, and colposcopy studies had unclear blinding of index test results. This led to a downgrade in evidence quality due to indirectness. Data for HPV testing followed by colposcopy with or without biopsy were calculated based on the sensitivity and specificity of the two tests, as direct data were not available. Diagnostic test accuracy data were based on women of unknown HIV status, and the data were not considered indirect, so the quality of evidence was not downgraded. In summary, the analysis highlights the variability in diagnostic accuracy and patient-important outcomes across different screening and treatment strategies for cervical cancer. The findings emphasize the need for high-quality evidence to guide clinical decision-making and optimize patient outcomes.
